Omar
O-mar
n. (proper, a duke of Edom; Hebrew, eloquent or a speaker)
Hebrew Owmar, from amar, to say — eloquent, a speaker. He is a son of Eliphaz the firstborn of Esau, and therefore a nephew of the Eliphaz who is not to be confused with Job's Temanite friend.

Biblical Definition

The sons of Esau's firstborn are listed: “And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz” (Genesis 36:11), and then given their titles: “These were dukes of the sons of Esau: the sons of Eliphaz the firstborn son of Esau; duke Teman, duke Omar, duke Zepho, duke Kenaz” (Genesis 36:15). The Chronicler repeats the roll and adds two names: “The sons of Eliphaz; Teman, and Omar, Zephi, and Gatam, Kenaz, and Timna, and Amalek” (1 Chronicles 1:36). Two of Omar's brothers matter enormously in later Scripture. Teman gives his name to the region from which Eliphaz the Temanite came to sit with Job, and Habakkuk sees God coming from Teman. Amalek, born of the concubine Timna, becomes the nation with whom the LORD swore he would have war from generation to generation.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a son of Eliphaz and a duke of the sons of Esau in the land of Edom.

expand to see more

ELOQUENT, a. Having the power of oratory; speaking with fluency, propriety, elegance and animation.

DUKE, n. A chief; a leader; in Scripture, the head of a family or clan among the Edomites.

TEMAN, n. A district of Edom, proverbial for wisdom; the home of Eliphaz the Temanite.

AMALEK, n. A grandson of Esau, and the nation descended from him, the first of the nations to fight Israel.

CONCUBINE, n. A woman who cohabits with a man without being his lawful wife; a secondary wife.

Key Scripture

Genesis 36:11 — "And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz."

Genesis 36:15 — "These were dukes of the sons of Esau: the sons of Eliphaz the firstborn son of Esau; duke Teman, duke Omar, duke Zepho, duke Kenaz,"

1 Chronicles 1:36 — "The sons of Eliphaz; Teman, and Omar, Zephi, and Gatam, Kenaz, and Timna, and Amalek."

Exodus 17:16 — "For he said, Because the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation."

Modern Corruption

Genealogies are skipped as filler, and with them the way Scripture quietly explains where later enemies came from — Amalek appears in a family list long before he appears in a battle.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What Omar's list teaches is how to read the registers. Five names in Genesis 36:11, of which Omar is one, and two more in the Chronicler's version: Timna and Amalek. Genesis explains that Timna was concubine to Eliphaz and bare him Amalek. That single clause in a skipped chapter is the origin of the nation that attacked the rear of Israel's column at Rephidim, picking off the feeble and the weary, and of whom the LORD said the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.

Teman, in the same list, runs the other way. It becomes a byword for wisdom — Jeremiah asks whether counsel is perished from Teman — and supplies Eliphaz the Temanite, the eldest of Job's comforters, and Habakkuk's vision of God coming from Teman with his glory covering the heavens. One father, one family list, and out of it comes both a proverb for wisdom and the archetype of the enemies of God's people. A reader who skips the genealogies loses the explanation of half the Old Testament's conflicts.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Owmar (H201), eloquent; amar (H559), to say; Teyman (H8487), Teman, the south; Amaleq (H6002), Amalek.

expand to see more

Hebrew Owmar (H201) — Omar, eloquent or a speaker; a duke of the sons of Esau.

Hebrew amar (H559) — to say, to speak; the root of the name.

Hebrew Eliyphaz (H464) — Eliphaz, God is his strength; Esau's firstborn, Omar's father.

Hebrew Teyman (H8487) — Teman, the south; his brother, and a byword for wisdom.

Hebrew Amaleq (H6002) — Amalek; born of Timna, and Israel's first enemy in arms.

Usage

"“The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz”."

"“Duke Teman, duke Omar” — the chiefs of Edom named."

"“Kenaz, and Timna, and Amalek” — an enemy born in a family list."
